summary:
Jigawa stands under Nigeria's national framework as well as its own state code. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide; Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Jigawa is one of twelve northern states in which Sharia has jurisdiction over criminal cases, and it is the only layer of criminal law that applies to Muslim residents for offences of this kind. Human Rights Watch (2004) traces the arrangement to Zamfara's governor, the first to extend Sharia to criminal law through the Sharia Establishment Law of 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000; by 2002 twelve northern states, Jigawa among them, had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and those twelve remain the only states where Sharia courts try criminal cases.

Jigawa's own instrument is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed into law on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). The UK Home Office (June 2025) lists Jigawa in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table under Sharia Penal Code (2000) and confirms that the Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa; the same note's section 8.2.20 sets out the Sharia codes in force in Kano, Borno, Kaduna and other states of the region.

The penalties Jigawa's code carries are severe and sex-specific. Married men face death by stoning; unmarried men face 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year; same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes with imprisonment of up to six months. Jigawa is one of four states, with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara, whose sodomy offence sets out those same terms, and Jigawa's code includes an 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence. The state code reaches conduct the federal statute does not reach, including women's same-sex conduct.

Entry and travel advice reflect that exposure. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.

Enforcement in Nigeria generally is not limited to the statute's text. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police who was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a risk that follows dating-app use into any state.
tangentialFactors:
Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression carries exposure. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Jigawa's exposure differs from that of the southern states in one structural respect: a visitor who is Muslim faces both the federal statute and a state penal code written expressly for sexual offences, while a visitor who is not Muslim faces the federal statute alone. The Sharia codes of Kano, Borno and Kaduna operate on the same model, so the pattern is regional rather than unique to Jigawa.

No Jigawa-specific enforcement record, prosecution, sentence or documented violence case against a trans or gender-nonconforming person appears in the inventory.
